{{short description|Every knot or link can be represented as a closed braid}}
[[File:An Element of the Braid Group.svg|thumb|This is a typical element of the braid group, which is used in the mathematical field of knot theory.]]

In mathematics '''Alexander's theorem''' states that every [[Knot (mathematics)|knot]] or [[Link (knot theory)|link]] can be represented as a [[Braid theory#Closed braids|closed]] [[Braid theory|braid]]; that is, a braid in which the corresponding ends of the strings are connected in pairs. The theorem is named after [[James Waddell Alexander II]], who published a proof in 1923.<ref>{{cite journal|first = James|last = Alexander| author-link=James Waddell Alexander II| title = A lemma on a system of knotted curves | journal = [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |volume = 9|issue=3|year = 1923|pages = 93–95|doi=10.1073/pnas.9.3.93|bibcode = 1923PNAS....9...93A|pmc = 1085274 | pmid=16576674|doi-access = free}}</ref>

Braids were first considered as a tool of [[knot theory]] by Alexander. His theorem gives a positive answer to the question ''Is it always possible to transform a given knot into a closed braid?'' A good construction example is found in [[Colin Adams (mathematician)|Colin Adams]]'s book.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Knot Book. Revised reprint of the 1994 original.|first=Colin C.|last = Adams|author-link=Colin Adams (mathematician)| publisher = [[American Mathematical Society]]|year=2004| location=Providence, RI| page = 130|isbn=0-8218-3678-1|mr=2079925}}</ref>

However, the correspondence between knots and braids is clearly not [[Bijection|one-to-one]]: a knot may have many braid representations. For example, conjugate braids yield equivalent knots. This leads to a second fundamental question: ''Which closed braids represent the same knot type?''
This question is addressed in [[Markov theorem|Markov's theorem]], which gives ‘moves’ relating any two closed braids that represent the same knot.
